runNotes: gpt-5.6-luna synthesis · gpt-5.4-nano planning · Tavily · MongoDB Atlas M0 · Vercel arn1

design.components: LUMINA has three deployed application components. The provided React UI runs on Vercel. A public Express gateway is the browser's only API endpoint. A private Express agent service runs the research loop, and a separate worker process from the same agent codebase handles document-indexing jobs. External dependencies are the OpenAI Responses API for planning and synthesis, Tavily or SerpApi, OpenAI embeddings, and one MongoDB Atlas database. The default answer model is configurable `gpt-5.6-luna`, a cost-first choice for this course proof of concept; quick requests use low reasoning effort and deep requests use medium effort. A separate configurable `gpt-5.4-nano` planner performs the narrow structured `plan_research` call without a reasoning phase, preserving model-generated decomposition while meeting the plan-latency budget at low cost. MongoDB also contains the jobs queue, persistent search cache, daily deep-usage counter, request records, and run records; GridFS stores uploads. Each answer additionally has request-local loop state and the agent keeps a disposable in-process LRU search cache. Local `runs/` JSON files are evidence consumed by the quality gates.
design.responsibilities:
The gateway alone may talk to the browser. It enforces `X-User-Id`, validates request bodies against the provided contract, assigns or reuses `X-Request-Id`, applies the ordinary traffic rate limit, logs the public request, proxies API calls, passes SSE through without buffering, and serves the built UI and generated evaluation report. It is never allowed to hold provider keys or decide whether AI spend is permitted.

The agent service alone may hold provider and MongoDB credentials, call the LLM/search/embedding providers, select tools, enforce per-depth loop limits, verify evidence, synthesize answers, persist user state, calculate cost, and authorize deep-search spend. The deep daily cap lives here because a cap in the gateway could be bypassed by another path to the spending component. The worker alone claims and performs document-indexing jobs. MongoDB is the durable source of truth; the UI and gateway do not own user or agent state.
design.communication:
The browser uses JSON HTTP for ordinary routes and SSE for an answer. Quick streams are `trace -> sources -> token -> done`; deep streams begin with `plan` before any retrieval. The gateway forwards the same contract and headers to the agent and propagates browser cancellation. A failure before streaming returns HTTP `502`; after SSE headers exist, the agent emits the contract `error` event with status `502`, records `terminated: "error"`, and closes the stream.

The API service enqueues document work by writing a MongoDB job, while the worker polls and claims jobs atomically. This makes upload acceptance fast and lets a stale claim be recovered after a crash. Provider calls use outbound HTTPS with deadlines tied to the loop's abort signal. If MongoDB is down, health is degraded and stateful operations fail loudly rather than pretending they succeeded.
design.state:
Authoritative state lives in MongoDB: threads, messages, explicit memories, Spaces, document metadata, chunks, jobs, requests, run records, persistent search results, and one internal deep-usage counter per user and UTC day. GridFS is authoritative for uploaded bytes. The daily counter is atomically reserved in the agent before planning or retrieval; concurrent requests cannot exceed the cap. A reservation is not released after a provider failure because provider cost may already have occurred and retries must not bypass the spend guard.

The LRU cache and in-flight loop coordinator are disposable. Search-cache rows are also non-authoritative and may expire without losing user data. Local run JSON is an exported evidence copy of the Mongo run record. Atlas search visibility is eventually consistent, so writing chunks does not make a document `indexed`; only a read-your-write probe that retrieves a new chunk permits that transition.
design.tradeoffs:
Splitting gateway and agent adds a network hop and two deployments, but it creates a clear trust boundary and keeps the key-bearing service private. Atlas Vector Search avoids synchronizing MongoDB with a second vector database and keeps citation text beside its locator, but accepts eventual index consistency and the free-tier search-index limit. A custom bounded loop around the OpenAI Responses API requires more bookkeeping than an agent framework, but makes tool eligibility, caps, trace order, costs, and termination directly testable. Planning and answer models remain separate environment choices so a small, low-latency model can handle constrained decomposition while Luna handles grounded synthesis; availability and price changes do not require architectural changes.

Document retrieval fuses independently ranked vector and text candidates with configurable reciprocal-rank fusion and top-k thresholds. A separate model reranker is deliberately omitted for this course-sized corpus: it would add latency, cost, and another provider failure point before the unmodified recall benchmark demonstrates that RRF is insufficient.

Deep sub-questions will use bounded parallelism rather than a simpler sequential loop. This reduces wall-clock time but makes shared tool-budget accounting and trace ordering harder. The design also consumes deep quota once an accepted request reserves it, even if a provider later fails; that can feel strict to a user, but releasing reservations would allow retry storms and could ignore cost already incurred. I am least certain about the initial fan-out concurrency: three is a conservative starting point, and it should be tuned from provider limits and measured latency without changing the external contract.

steps.error: tavily search failed with HTTP 401: {"detail":{"error":"Unauthorized: missing or invalid API key."}}

failing.notes: A deliberately invalid Tavily key made web_search record the upstream HTTP 401 and terminate error with zero answer tokens, proving the system fails loud instead of returning a plausible fallback.
